paras: The killing of Josephus Fairchild took place on September 13, 1881, in Lake Charles, Louisiana, when deputy sheriffs shot a Black prisoner who broke from their custody minutes after he was sentenced to death for murder. Struck in the head by a deputy's rifle ball, he died in the parish jail that night, and a coroner's jury found the officers justified. Both Lake Charles weeklies described the escape at length, and the story ran across the country as a wire brief and as a reprinted narrative titled "A Race for Life".

At the opening of the September term of the district court, the grand jury indicted Fairchild, described by the Echo as "a short but strongly built negro," for the murder of a Black man named Frank Clout near Lake Charles the previous spring. After the killing he had gone to Rapides Parish, where the sheriff arrested him and held him at Alexandria until Deputy Sheriff John S. Hawkins brought him back to the Lake Charles jail. A jury, kept by Hawkins from a Saturday evening to a Monday evening, convicted him by an unqualified verdict in early September.

The Commercial reported that on the road from Alexandria Fairchild told Hawkins he had ridden for several years with John Wesley Hardin, and that he had taken his surname from his first employer in the parish, George Fairchild.

Just before noon on the last day of the term, Fairchild was brought into court with his handcuffs and shackles removed and was sentenced to death by District Judge S. D. Read. Four deputy sheriffs attended him, one of them, Richard Coward, carrying a Winchester rifle and the others pistols, because, according to the Commercial, he was known to be a desperate character. As a deputy led him out by the arm, he threw off the grip on the first of the front steps and ran around the corner of the courthouse.

Coward and another deputy fired as he crossed the roadside ditch, and a shot hit him in the leg near the knee. He rose and ran up the street past the jail "amid a perfect storm of bullets," then turned down Ryan street, where a ball from Coward's rifle struck him behind the left ear and came out at the face. He was carried to the jail and lay unconscious until between ten and eleven o'clock that night, when he died; the Echo, citing the physician's finding that the skull was not fractured, attributed his death to concussion of the brain.

A coroner's jury, sitting before a justice of the peace acting as coroner, found that Fairchild died of gun and pistol wounds inflicted by the guards while he was attempting to escape, and that the officers were justified. No report of any further action concerning the deputies appears in the coverage.

The two Lake Charles papers reported the killing in their September 17 issues and treated it as the end of a lawful case. The Echo called the escape "a thrilling scene from real life" and closed with the inquest verdict that justified killing a prisoner "escaping from legal custody," while its court roundup listed Fairchild's death sentence among the term's results. The Commercial printed the inquest verdict in full and argued that his running from armed men proved him a desperate character.

Northern papers carried only a two-sentence brief among crime items, naming him Joseph Fairchild, "a powerfully built negro" in Lancaster and "a negro murderer" in Concord, who "soon fell dead, riddled with bullets." The Echo's narrative traveled further under the title "A Race for Life," credited to the New Orleans Picayune in the Dallas Daily Herald on September 23 and to the Echo in Wisconsin weeklies in October, with the subhead "Desperate Attempt of a Louisiana Murderer to Escape from Four Officers."

The wire brief has Fairchild falling dead under a hail of bullets, but both local accounts say he was hit in the leg, kept running, was struck in the head, and died hours later in the jail. The reprints place the sentencing on "last Friday," while the Echo's own issue and its court roundup put it on Tuesday, the last day of the term.

bases: Deputy sheriffs guarding a sentenced prisoner shot him as he ran from the courthouse, and a rifle ball fired by one of them killed him; no crowd took part (A3, A5, A6).

The two Lake Charles weeklies, the Echo and the Commercial, give separate accounts that agree on the sentence, the break at the courthouse steps, the shooting by deputies and the inquest verdict, and a wire brief carried the core event north (A3, A5, A6).

accounts.label: Lake Charles Echo
accounts.gist: Fairchild threw off a deputy's grasp on the courthouse steps and ran; Coward and another deputy fired, he fell, rose and ran on 'amid a perfect storm of bullets' until Coward's rifle ball struck his head on Ryan street; he died that night, and the coroner's jury justified the killing.

accounts.label: Lake Charles Commercial
accounts.gist: Four armed deputies were detailed because he was known as a desperate character; he upset the deputy holding him, was hit in the leg and then in the head by a Winchester ball, was examined at the jail by two physicians who did not think the wound dangerous, and died; the inquest found the officers justified.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: He broke from the guards when brought in for sentence, ran up the street, and the officers fired until he 'soon fell dead, riddled with bullets.'

framing.detail: The Echo told the escape as 'a thrilling scene from real life' and reported without comment the coroner's verdict that the killing of a prisoner 'escaping from legal custody' was justified.

The Commercial called him 'a desperate character', offered his flight from armed men as proof of it, printed the inquest verdict exonerating the officers, and headed the story with words that appear to read 'From a Rifle Ball Instead of the Gallows'.
Northern papers ran a two-sentence brief among crime items calling him 'a powerfully built negro' or 'a negro murderer' who fell 'riddled with bullets'.
The Echo narrative circulated as 'A Race for Life', in Texas credited to the New Orleans Picayune and in Wisconsin subheaded 'Desperate Attempt of a Louisiana Murderer to Escape from Four Officers'.
